chunks: "Assembly is a low-level programming language that maps almost one-to-one onto the machine instructions a specific processor executes.
Instead of writing the binary instruction, you write a mnemonic like add t0, t1, t2 or lw t2, 0(a0) , and an assembler translates it to the binary encoding.
Because it's tied to the instruction set, RISC-V assembly, ARM assembly and x86 assembly are all different languages.
Compared with C, assembly has no types, no loops or functions as such, and no portability. I handle registers, memory addresses, the stack and branches myself.
A single C line like sum += a[i] becomes several instructions: a load, an add, and pointer updates.
C is compiled to assembly and then to machine code, so one C source can target many processors, and the compiler does the register allocation and optimization for me.
It's interpreted: the interpreter, itself a program compiled to machine code, executes Python bytecode, so a simple addition involves many machine instructions and runtime type checks.
That's why Python is great for scripts and test automation, but not for a tight loop on a microcontroller.

I'd say assembly is for when I need exact control: boot code after reset, interrupt entry and context switching, hand-tuned kernels, and especially reading disassembly to debug or to see what the compiler did with my C."
